title: Yesterday’s cooking oil powers 410,000 pink winter sakura lights along Tokyo’s Meguro River
description: Who says you have to wait until spring for cherry blossoms? A wide river coated in pink petals, adorned on either side by rows of stunningly gorgeous cherry blossom trees amid a sprawling cityscape, the Meguro River in spring is one of Tokyo’s must-see sakura viewing spots. Running through the neighborhoods of Gotanda and Osaki, […]
content:
Who says you have to wait until spring for cherry blossoms?

A wide river coated in pink petals, adorned on either side by rows of stunningly gorgeous cherry blossom trees amid a sprawling cityscape, the Meguro River in spring is one of Tokyo’s must-see sakura viewing spots. Running through the neighborhoods of Gotanda and Osaki, this two-kilometer (1.2-mile) stretch of sakura trees creates of massive pink canopy for visitors to enjoy, and most Tokyo guidebooks will feature a photo of this iconic spot.

Although not every trip to Tokyo coincides with the blossoms, landing a few months earlier in December or January means you don’t necessarily have to miss out on appreciating this pink scenery—it’ll just be LEDs instead of actual petals.

▼ That’s not to say there aren’t different cherry blossom varieties at other times of the year, like around November at Senmi Shikizakura no Sato in Aichi.

Every winter, the Meguro area hosts the Meguro River Minna no Illumination, turning the once bare cherry branches along the river into a glowing pink ‘winter sakura’ display. Running from December 4 to January 31, between 5:00 p.m. and 10:00 p.m., around 410,000 pink lights will be stretched across the riverbanks, creating a sensory clash as the warming sight of the pink trees battles with the cold of the winter air.

There are many people who eschew winter illuminations due to its environmental impact, but this light display operates on a 100-percent self-generated, closed-loop energy system powered by recycled biodiesel. Local restaurants, businesses, and neighborhood households collect their used cooking oil throughout the year, which gets refined to power the generators, meaning that the oil that may have been used to cook your dinner the previous night might be contributing to tonight’s stroll along the river.

▼ Gotanda Station (五反田駅) is the uppermost landmark on the map, with the yellow Gotanda Waterfront Plaza (五反田ふれあい水辺広場) marked just below it, and the stretch of sakura trees running down to the southeast past Osaki Station (大崎駅).

Along with the lights, the area around Gotanda Waterfront Plaza (a three-minute walk from Gotanda Station) will also feature an interactive light-ripple art installation by creative unit Zero by Zero, which is also powered by the same biodiesel (tentatively available until December 31), and community recycling pop-ups.

A small opening-day ceremony with local school bands and riverboats will be held at 4:00 p.m. on December 4, but between 10:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m. a hands-on workshop to make your own kaleidoscope using waste materials such as cardboard and paper tubes will allow you discover new charms in familiar scenery.

If you’re out exploring the area over the holidays, taking a brisk walk under a couple hundred thousand glowing pink lights is a great way to experience the joy of spring a couple of months early.

title: Life-size Gundam head going on display in Osaka, hopefully will find permanent home
description: Gundam head arrives in Osaka ahead of Gundam Base. Its case rests largely on compliance with criteria related to population, economic importance, and geography, but soon Osaka will be […]
content:
Gundam head arrives in Osaka ahead of Gundam Base.

Osaka has been making a big push recently to obtain official status as Japan’s backup capital should a major disaster knock out government facilities in Tokyo. Its case rests largely on compliance with criteria related to population, economic importance, and geography, but soon Osaka will be able to boast yet another fine feature: the full-size head of Gundam on display within the city.

The head unit of the iconic anime mecha was first seen in Yokohama, where it sat on the shoulders of the life-size RX-78F00 Gundam at the Gundam Factory Yokohama. The 18-meter (59-foot) tall statue was removed in the spring of 2024 and relocated to Osaka for the Expo 2025 world’s fair, serving as the centerpiece of the Gundam Next Future Pavilion. With the Expo finished, the RX-78F00/E (as the updated Osaka version of the statue was called) has been dismantled, but the head will be going on display at the new Lucua South entertainment complex in Osaka’s Umeda neighborhood next month.

▼ The head, which will be displayed on the building’s 10th floor, stands 2.2 meters tall and weighs approximately 370 kilograms (815.7 pounds), so there’s little chance of anyone running off with it.

The head is just one part of a planned proliferation of Gundam fun coming to Lucua South. Scheduled to open in February of next year is a brand-new Gundam Base Osaka specialty shop, filled with Gunpla plastic model kits and other merch. As a touch of local flavor, Gundam’s spherical mascot robot Haro will get a makeover to make him look like a takoyaki octopus dumpling, Osaka’s representative street food snack.

▼ The takoyaki Haro will talk too, but there’s no word yet on whether or not he’ll speak in the distinctive Osaka dialect of Japanese.

Anime fan shoppers won’t have to wait all the way until February, though, as high-end figure brand Tamashii Nations will also be opening a new branch in Lucua South on December 2, with statues of the original Gundam and Dragon Ball’s Goku greeting visitors.

▼ A figure of the RX-78F00/E, in the pose it struck during the Expo, will be on offer.

Two days later, on December 4, an official Gundam Card Game store will also open inside the building…

…and fashionable fans of anime mecha can get their fix the soonest of all, with a Strict-G store, stocked with items from the Gundam apparel/accessory line of the same name, opening in Lucua South on November 24.

▼ Two new Osaka Gundam Yokosuka jackets will be available, one with an image of Osaka Castle, the other with the city’s name written in kanji characters.

Getting back to the Gundam head, though the display starts on December 4, there’s currently no announced end date. Common sense would suggest that it’ll be on display at least until the Gundam Base Osaka opens in February, and it’s hard to imagine a better place for it to remain after that than in the store itself, but still, checking it out sooner rather than later is probably the smart move.

title: Tokyo police arrest the Ame-zing Spider-Man
description: Your unfriendly rainy-day Spider-Man. For nearly a decade, Tokyo had been terrorized by a wall-crawling bandit who would climb into the higher floors of buildings and make off with whatever cash or valuables he could get his sticky fingers on. His name was Yuki Horiguchi, but to police, he’s known as the Ame-zing Spider-Man. That’s […]
content:
Your unfriendly rainy-day Spider-Man.

For nearly a decade, Tokyo had been terrorized by a wall-crawling bandit who would climb into the higher floors of buildings and make off with whatever cash or valuables he could get his sticky fingers on. His name was Yuki Horiguchi, but to police, he’s known as the Ame-zing Spider-Man.

That’s not a typo in his nickname. The Japanese word for “rain” is “ame” (ah-may), and this Spider-Man’s MO was to strike on rainy days in particular. Likely relying on the fact that people tend to not look up when it’s raining, Horiguchi would access the roofs of buildings using emergency stairs on the outside, and then rappel down to a window, breaking through it to access the building and burglarize it.

This is what he did on one rainy day in December 2025. Climbing down a rope and gaining entry to the sixth-floor balcony of a head spa in Taito, he stole a portable safe and a wallet before moving to an adjacent building and stealing about 110,000 yen (US$690) in cash.

It isn’t clear how police managed to catch the Ame-zing Spider-Man this time, but the thing about getting a cool nickname from the police is that they know exactly when it’s you who committed a crime. Horiguchi had already been picked up by law enforcement in 2019 for similar burglaries on rainy days, so it isn’t taking much to link this and some 50 other incidents in the Greater Tokyo Area over the past year alone to Spidey.

Many readers of the news online took serious issue with a criminal being given the honorable name of “Spider-Man.”

“He should apologize to the real Spider-Man!”
“Normally, I’d say talented criminals should put their skills toward doing good work, but this guy kind of seems really cut out to be a burglar more than anything.”
“Giving him a name like that shows a complete lack of sincerity towards the victims.”
“He doesn’t deserve the name Spider-Man.”
“50 times?! They can’t let that slide.”
“That’s lame.”
“The cop who came up with ‘Ame-zing Spider-Man’ should be arrested too.”
“I wonder if Sony will complain about this.”
“Seems like a lot of effort and risk for 110,000 yen.”
“More like Lupin III than Spider-Man.”
“He doesn’t have any mutant powers. He’s just a bad Daredevil.”

It seems rather likely that this repeat offender will be spending a lot of time behind bars. Perhaps he can learn there that with a great nickname comes great attention from the police, and finally knock it off with this life of crime.

title: Ichiran releases an at-home counter kit that turns your desk into a ramen restaurant
description: Iconic ramen chain brings out an exclusive product so you can fully focus on the taste of the noodles. Amongst all the many ramen restaurants in Japan, Ichiran stands out for its unique dining experience, where customers sit at a long counter with private partitions and receive their noodles through a bamboo screen. The unusual […]
content:
Iconic ramen chain brings out an exclusive product so you can fully focus on the taste of the noodles.

Amongst all the many ramen restaurants in Japan, Ichiran stands out for its unique dining experience, where customers sit at a long counter with private partitions and receive their noodles through a bamboo screen. The unusual seating layout is what the chain calls its “Aji Shuuchuu Counter”, or “Taste Concentration Counter”, as the private seating allows you to concentrate solely on the taste of the noodles, free from the gaze of others around you.

Now, the chain is giving us a way to enjoy the special dining setup at home, with the release of an exclusive “Taste Concentration Counter Kit”. We were fortunate enough to receive one in the office recently, so our reporter Ahiruneko got straight to trying it out, using the kit to turn his desk into an Ichiran restaurant.

The kit requires some assembly, so Ahiruneko started by inserting the side panels into the overhead sign and countertop pieces.

▼ Then he attached the reinforcement parts…

▼ …and finished by inserting the bamboo blind into the back of the setup.

▼ Now he was ready to eat!

The Taste Concentration Counter turned out to be tiny, but it displayed impressive attention to detail, with the front sign covered in explanatory text and the bamboo blind raising and lowering as it would at an actual restaurant.

▼ It even came with the side sign details, which includes instructions on how to place your order.

The most impressive thing, however, turned out to be the call button, because when you press it, you hear the same familiar chime played in Ichiran restaurants!

It was far more Ichiran-like than Ahiruneko had expected, allowing him to realise his dreams of opening a totally new branch of the chain in the office, which he dubbed the “Ichiran SoraNews24” branch.

▼ It may not be the most impressive branch, but it’s certainly a fun one.

Ahiruneko couldn’t help but smile upon opening his tiny branch, which consisted of one counter seat, set up neatly on his desk.

The only thing missing from the kit was a tiny chef to go with it, so Ahiruneko stepped in to take on noodle-cooking duties.

With everyone else in the office engrossed in their writing, Ahiruneko continued running the branch on his own, and when he lifted the bamboo screen, he felt a rush of excitement at what was to come.

▼ Ta daaaa! A hot bowl of Ichiran ramen!

Even though he was the one serving himself, Ahiruneko loved the setup, and was impressed at how the opening was just wide enough for the ramen bowl to fit perfectly.

Now he had the ideal ramen-eating setup on his desk, where he could concentrate entirely on the bowl in front of him…

▼ …without worrying about his boss and colleagues staring at him.

The Taste Concentration Counter was the perfect sanctuary where he could remain blissfully unaware of any potential side-eye from his higher-up colleague (上司) and company president (社長).

To really get into the Ichiran mood, you need to hunch over and slurp your noodles, so that’s exactly what Ahiruneko did.

By removing everything other than the counter from his field of vision, he was able to trick his brain into thinking he was actually at Ichiran.

Though he looked a bit like a student hiding a snack behind an upright textbook, the Flavour Concentration Counter Kit is enclosed by walls on three sides, so the chances of anyone noticing his noodle moment remained extremely low.

Even the workmate opposite him would never dream that he was having an Ichiran experience right there in the office.

▼ Hunched over a laptop? Or a bowl of noodles?

It didn’t take long for Ahiruneko to finish all his noodles, but as there was still some broth left, he did what any noodle lover should do at this point.

▼ He pressed the call button to order a noodle refill (known as “kaedama” in Japanese).

▼ Leaping up to attend to his own order, Ahiruneko headed over to the kitchen to boil up his kaedama.

▼ Then, back at his desk, the bamboo blind went up.


▼ And in came his extra serving of noodles!

▼ Ahiruneko, playing the role of both staff and customer with equal amounts of joy.

For Ahiruneko, a visit to Ichiran isn’t complete until you’ve ordered a noodle refill, so he was thrilled that he could recreate this ideal visit from the comfort of his office desk.

title: Move aside, Asahi Super Dry – Asahi Spice Beer is in town, and it’s hotter than you think
description: Meet the surprisingly fiery beer that’s on everyone’s lips right now. When a lot of overseas people think about Japanese beer, Japan’s world-famous brand “Asahi Super Dry” might come to mind. However, right now, there’s a new type of Asahi making news in Japan, and rather than being dry, it’s surprisingly fiery, as the brew […]
content:
Meet the surprisingly fiery beer that’s on everyone’s lips right now.

When a lot of overseas people think about Japanese beer, Japan’s world-famous brand “Asahi Super Dry” might come to mind. However, right now, there’s a new type of Asahi making news in Japan, and rather than being dry, it’s surprisingly fiery, as the brew is made with jalapenos.

Called Asahi Spice Beer, you can find the new tipple at convenience stores, supermarkets, and liquor shops, the latter of which is where we found ours, being sold in 350-millilitre (12-ounce) cans for 195 yen, (US$1.22)…

▼ …and six-packs for 1,094 yen.

Released on 21 October, after being test-marketed in 2024, the beer is already proving to be popular, as we had to visit six stores to find it. It immediately caught our eye from the shelf, with its red-hot hue and fiery details, and the words “Brewed from quality beer ingredients and jalapeno pepper” under the golden name, “Asahi Spice Beer“.

After hearing from a friend that the beer didn’t have too much of a kick to it, we didn’t feel that we had anything to worry about with the heat levels in the drink. After all, how spicy can a beer be?

▼ With that thought in mind, we popped open the can.

Pouring some of it into a glass, it looked like an ordinary beer, and there wasn’t any noticeable spicy aroma.

▼ Feeling unsure of what to expect, we raised the glass and took a sip, only to find…

▼ … it was spicy!!

Though we’d only taken a tiny sip, the heat was unmistakable. This wasn’t a case of mild spiciness, as our friend had suggested, because within seconds, our tongue, lips and throat began to tingle.

It was a reaction that took us completely by surprise, and what was even more unexpected was the flavour, as it was utterly delicious. The first thing you taste is the crispness and umami you’d expect from a good beer, with just the right amount of bitterness, and then the heat from the jalapenos comes bolting in, lingering in the carbonation and leaving you with a sense of refreshment and spiciness at the same time.

Rather than getting in the way of things, the jalapenos actually added a nice accent in flavour. That said, there were moments when the heat lingered longer than expected, but after trying the beer with food, the heat took on another dimension.

Trying it with a bowl of oden, the spice beer became even more refreshing, with the heat bringing out the flavours of the simmered ingredients.

Usually, eating spicy food makes us want to drink more beer, but this time it was the other way around – drinking the beer made us want to eat more oden. Together, they worked a treat, and after dinner, the beer went well with a square of dark chocolate too.

After trying the beer, we were reminded that life really is better with a little spice. And the spice in this beer is nothing to sneeze at, as it’s a stimulating tipple that’ll enliven your entire palate with every sip.

In fact, once you’ve had one of these, you might find yourselves like us, hankering for another. The release is well-timed too, as it’s a surprisingly good winter warmer, so be sure to keep an eye out for it next time you’re browsing the aisles in Japan.

title: “Sweet sake” with yuzu is coming to Japan’s wonderful world of hot canned drinks this winter
description: Morinaga goes to Kochi in its search for a new spin on a traditional Japanese winter drink. Japan is a country that really gets into the spirit of each season, and not just in terms of fashions and festivals. As we get into the back half of autumn, more and more hot drinks start appearing […]
content:
Morinaga goes to Kochi in its search for a new spin on a traditional Japanese winter drink.

Japan is a country that really gets into the spirit of each season, and not just in terms of fashions and festivals. As we get into the back half of autumn, more and more hot drinks start appearing in convenience stores and vending machines. You can always count on hot coffee and green tea to always make an appearance, but each year also brings a selection of new entries into this warming, relaxing segment of the drink market, and one that we’ll be seeing soon is yuzu amazake.

Amazake literally translates as “sweet sake,” and yes, just like conventional sake, it’s a beverage made from fermented rice. Aside from that, though, amazake bears little resemblance to its more internationally famous rice wine cousin. For one thing, amazake is non-alcoholic. It’s also opaque and thicker in consistency, sort of a rice-based smoothie with a sweet flavor.

Though it can be drunk cold, amazake’s consistency makes it especially well-suited to heating up on a cold winter’s day so that it can warm you up from the inside. Japanese confectionery and beverage maker Morinaga has been selling canned amazake for many years, but they’ll be trying something new this winter with Kin no Kaoru Amazake Yuzu (“Golden Scent Amazake Yuzu”). The customary rich, sweet amazake flavor here gets an added twist with the introduction of a little touch of yuzu juice, sourced from Japan’s most prestigious producer of the sweetly sharp citrus fruit, Kochi Prefecture. The result, Morinaga says, is a fragrant, sweet, and soothing concoction that’s perfect for when you need to take a break and reward yourself as you’re crossing things off your to-do list ahead of the end-of-the-year holiday season.

Kin no Kaoru Amazake Yuzu goes on sale December 1.

title: KFC now sells takikomi gohan rice boxes in Japan, if you know where to look for them [Taste test]
description: Kenta creates a new way to enjoy its Original Recipe: with chopsticks! “Kenta Rice Box” might sound like an offering from a traditional Japanese restaurant, but Kenta is actually short for “Kentakki,” the Japanese pronunciation of “Kentucky,” as in Kentucky Fried Chicken. Yes, like McDonalds (“Makku” or “Makudo”) and Starbucks (“Sutaba”), KFC has become so […]
content:
Kenta creates a new way to enjoy its Original Recipe: with chopsticks!

“Kenta Rice Box” might sound like an offering from a traditional Japanese restaurant, but Kenta is actually short for “Kentakki,” the Japanese pronunciation of “Kentucky,” as in Kentucky Fried Chicken. Yes, like McDonalds (“Makku” or “Makudo”) and Starbucks (“Sutaba”), KFC has become so popular in Japan that it’s got its own fan nickname, which is also a sign that there’s room for some special Japan-exclusive menu items tailored to local tastes, the newest of which is the Kenta Rice Box.

Part of the design concept for the Kenta Rice Box is to be “a KFC meal you can eat with chopsticks.” This would seem to go against the chain’s well-known promise of being “finger-lickin’ good,” but we weren’t going to knock the Kenta Rice Box until we’d tried it, so that’s just what we headed out to do.

Currently, the Kenta Rice Box is available only at select KFC Japan branches in Tokyo and the prefectures of Kanagawa, Saitama, Chiba, Osaka, and Hyogo (a full list can be found here), but luckily we didn’t have to go too far out of our way to find it for sale here in the capital. Prices also vary by region, starting at 690 yen (US$4.35), but the downtown Tokyo branch we got ours at was charging 740 yen for the Kenta Rice Box alone, or 930 yen as a combo with a drink.

Opening up the flaps, the first thing you’ll see is sliced pieces of boneless fried chicken slathered with a teriyaki sauce. This is actually still KFC Original Recipe chicken, though, so you get an internationalized mix of its familiar herbs and spices plus all the sweet and savory notes of teriyaki, which makes for a very tasty combination.

Underneath the chicken is a layer of shredded cabbage, giving you some nice crisp texture, and underneath that is the rice. This isn’t just any rice, though. It’s takikomi gohan, a traditional Japanese dish made by cooking white rice in a pot together with other seasonings or ingredients, so that the additional flavor gets steeped in. Fitting, for the Kenta Rice Box KFC Japan makes its takikomigohan with chicken broth.

Though the takikomi gohan flavor isn’t particularly heavy, it is really good, giving the rice a delicious touch of meatiness that pairs very nicely with the pieces of fried chicken themselves.

As for negatives, with fried chicken being their specialty, we tend to associate KFC with large, hearty meals, but the Kenta Rice Box isn’t particularly huge. It’s definitely bigger than a snack, but this isn’t the sort of thing that, if you ate it at lunch, would have you thinking a simple salad or something is all you’re going to need for dinner later on. Also, despite the design goal of being something you can eat with chopsticks, the unusual shape of the box, squared-off at the top but round at its base, actually makes it a little hard to eat with utensils, and we think a spoon might actually be the better equipment to use.

But out of “tastes great,” “large portion,” and “easy to eat with chopsticks,” we’d say the first is the most important, and that’s a box the Kenta Rice Box easily checks.

title: Japan’s upcoming Romancecar train seeks to end intimacy with its super-wide seats
description: Odakyu’s sleek new train features droplet windows, spacious seating, and a driver sitting above your head. With the varied lineup of in-service carriages and impeccable punctuality, the Japanese train system could be said to be an art form, but the train companies are not ones to rest on their laurels, constantly seeking improvements to their […]
content:
Odakyu’s sleek new train features droplet windows, spacious seating, and a driver sitting above your head.

With the varied lineup of in-service carriages and impeccable punctuality, the Japanese train system could be said to be an art form, but the train companies are not ones to rest on their laurels, constantly seeking improvements to their services. Odakyu Electric Railway recently unveiled plans for its next-generation limited express train, the Type 80000, which is due to debut in March 2029. This new model will adopt one of the company’s most known monikers: the Romancecar.

Despite what the name might imply, the Romancecar service is not targeted at young lovers hoping to get some quick private time as they hurtle along the tracks. Instead, the name derives from ‘romance seats’, the type of paired seating with no middle armrest to separate the two chairs.

▼ True romance seat style.

Other train companies started to use the name, but Odakyu later went on to register the trademark Romancecar for their tourist-heavy limited express trains. Now the Romancecar fleet can be seen shipping thousands of tourists back and forth between Shinjuku and popular sightseeing destinations of Hakone, the hot spring haven with stunning views of Mt. Fuji, and the coastal sights of Enoshima.

One thing that makes these trains popular among railway enthusiasts is its observation seating, where the driver sits in a raised compartment above the passengers, allowing for the front row to have a completely unobstructed view of the countryside rushing by.

▼ View from the front row.

The upcoming Type 80000 will embrace this feature, along with a couple of extra design decisions to make travel more enjoyable for its passengers. The car bodies will sport a blue-green finish and their design will be centered around the theme of ‘water.’

▼ The new model has over 280 standard seats.

Many travelers out for the day or the weekend may often find themselves playing an apologetic game of spatial Tetris with their knees and luggage as they try to avoid inconveniencing other passengers, so Odakyu has decided to tackle this problem with extra-wide ‘spacious seats.’ Measuring roughly 60 centimeters across (23.6 inches), and among the widest on any Japanese train, these seats are designed so you can stretch out, work, or simply exist without getting intimately familiar with your neighbor’s elbow.

For small groups or families, one car will feature four-person booths situated beside large, 1.8-meter (70.9-inch) circular windows shaped like water droplets.

With glass stretching from almost floor to ceiling, and gently curved partitions that separate the booths from the rest of the carriage, the booth seats will allow you and your group to focus on all of nature’s beauty as it rolls past the window.

Just remember: despite the Romancecar name, this new model will not guarantee a deeper level of intimacy with your partner. However, with seats that wide and windows that big, you might just end up falling in love with the train instead.

title: Yakuza boss sues expressway owners for discrimination against criminals
description: You gotta fight for your right to be a party to a contract. Ever since 2011, things have been getting rougher and rougher for members of organized crime groups in Japan. That was when a law was passed prohibiting companies from entering into contracts with any known member. That’s why any time you sign up […]
content:
You gotta fight for your right to be a party to a contract.

Ever since 2011, things have been getting rougher and rougher for members of organized crime groups in Japan. That was when a law was passed prohibiting companies from entering into contracts with any known member. That’s why any time you sign up for a phone or point card, you have to declare on it whether or not you belong to such a group.

And with just about everything shifting from cash-based purchases to cashless subscriptions, members of groups such as the yakuza are in an increasingly tight situation. 

One example can be found on Japan’s many privately owned expressways that require a toll to drive on. It is expected that all toll boths will end cash toll payments in favor of the ETC card system by 2030. An ETC card is like an auxiliary credit card that hooks up directly to your car and is detected automatically as you enter and leave an expressway, billing you the appropriate amount. You need to sign up for one much like you do with a credit card, which means yakuza cannot.

Feeling his freedom of movement was hindered by this, a senior yakuza member filed a lawsuit against the operators of expressways, such as NEXCO East, for discrimination. According to the suit, in July 2023, the plaintiff attempted to apply for a special ETC Personal Card that doesn’t require a credit card to use, because he can’t get one of those either. On the application was a checkbox that should be marked if the applicant is a member of an organized crime group. The plaintiff just crossed that whole section out and filled in the rest of the application properly. He was notified a month later that his application was denied.

On 10 November, a ruling was handed down in Fukuoka District Court, wherein Judge Masakatsu Tange dismissed the lawsuit, saying that by not being able to use expressways, the restrictions on his rights and freedoms were very minor. 

In Japan, these roads are completely optional, and it is possible to take similar routes to anywhere in the country. The only major benefits are a lack of traffic lights that will generally ensure a swifter arrival than regular city streets. So, the judge is right in that regard. The yakuza member’s ability to go places is more inconvenienced than it is obstructed.

▼ Though in his defense, the sheer number of red lights on regular streets in Japan is rather maddening.

There’s a strange kind of irony to see the yakuza trying to settle matters in a court of law. He also has a point that these restrictive laws against people like him are technically discriminatory, but the matter boils down to whether society deems it right to discriminate against criminals or not. Most online comments regarding this story seem to agree that it is right.

“Just walk then.”
“He’s not really a credible plaintiff, after all.”
“Maybe he should just stop doing illegal stuff?”
“That’s on him.”
“They’re free to leave that life behind, aren’t they?”
“What is this guy talking about? It’s not like he follows the law.”
“They shouldn’t even be allowed to have driver’s licenses.”
“Even with that kind of ETC card, he’d need a bank account, so how did he get that? Or a lawyer, for that matter?”

This law prohibiting doing business with organized crime groups was enacted in 2011, meaning before that it was possible for members to open bank accounts and do lots of other things. That’s why you might see a yakuza member using an old flip phone, because they’re contractually stuck in that era’s tech. Also, many people get bank accounts at a young age, likely before they enter a life of crime.

As for hiring a lawyer, that is a constitutional right that cannot be denied, so crime groups are allowed to enter into contracts with attorneys as an exception. That’s also why they can receive medical care, which is also a business transaction but guaranteed by law. Public utility providers also cannot refuse service to anyone by law, but yakuza members technically aren’t allowed to buy property, so I’m not sure where they’ll hook it up.

Still, it’s definitely a pain in the butt being a member of the yakuza these days, and by design. It just goes to show that all the goons in the world can’t save you from a passive-aggressive bureaucracy.

title: KFC Japan starts selling soft-serve ice cream at select locations, and they’ve even put it in a biscuit
description: There are many ways to enjoy this new sweet dessert, including as a dip for fried chicken. KFC is world-famous for its fried chicken, but right now it’s turning heads for something else in Japan, with the release of soft-serve ice cream. While that would be big news on its own, what’s even more impressive […]
content:
There are many ways to enjoy this new sweet dessert, including as a dip for fried chicken.

KFC is world-famous for its fried chicken, but right now it’s turning heads for something else in Japan, with the release of soft-serve ice cream. While that would be big news on its own, what’s even more impressive is the fact that the chain is also sandwiching the soft serve inside a biscuit, creating a brand new dessert on the menu.

Available only at select locations, we sent our ice-cream-loving reporter Mr Sato over to our nearest participating branch in Tokyo’s Akihabara to check it out as soon as we heard about it.

▼ Upon arriving, he saw this sign outside, which made him think “When the heck did this happen!?”

It really is an under-the-radar release, with information about it scarcely available online, and after asking staff about it, Mr Sato learned that sales only began in late October. Though Mr Sato thought it was a shame that sales hadn’t begun earlier in summer, he certainly wasn’t complaining, and after mulling over the three soft serve cones available – vanilla, chocolate and a mix of both for 290 yen (US$1.81) each – he decided to opt for the “Biscuit & Soft-Serve Drink Set” for 680 yen.

After placing his order, Mr Sato began to fret as he realised that the warm biscuit might make the soft serve melt faster than usual, which isn’t ideal for someone with the responsibility of photographing the dessert. Determined to get the best photos possible, he rubbed his hands together and prepared his fingers for some fast snapping, which meant that when it arrived, he was ready to grab a selfie with the new dessert.

Wasting no time, he turned the camera back towards the dessert, which looked gloriously sinful, but peering closer, he realised that…

▼ …the ice cream already seemed to be melting from the heat of the biscuit.

As an experienced soft-serve eater, Mr Sato knows that a variety of factors affect the melting rate of ice cream, including the milk fat content and the amount of air incorporated into it. With this variety looking both milky and airy, he had little time to waste, so he dipped his spoon in for a taste.

The flavour was very simple and not particularly strong, giving him neither an especially good nor bad impression. Personally, he thought that Family Mart’s soft-serve actually had more flavour, and was an arguably better deal at just 298 yen, even for the Giga Size.

▼ Still, the creaminess was great, and the ice cream isn’t designed to be eaten on its own, so he tried it with the biscuit.

The combination of warm, crispy biscuit and soft-serve ice cream was a winning one. The contrast between crunchiness and meltiness was irresistible, and though you can eat them together as a sort of ice cream sandwich, he found that dipping the biscuit into the soft-serve proved to be another great way to enjoy it.

Using the soft serve as a dip turned out to be such a good idea that he decided to try it with some of the other items on the menu.

▼ French fry and soft serve = heaven.

After trying the chip dip, it was time to move onto bigger fry, quite literally, with a fried chicken dip. You’d be forgiven for thinking Mr Sato may have gone too far with this idea, but he genuinely recommends giving this combination a try. The sweetness of the cream brings out the savoury saltiness and spices of the chicken, making it taste even better.

This unusual but delicious combo reminded Mr Sato of chicken and waffles – popular in the American South, the home of fried chicken – which combines fried chicken with maple syrup.

▼ That thought reminded him that the dessert came with honey maple syrup, so he wasted no time in pouring it over.

▼ The soft serve was now disappearing fast, so after snapping a couple of shots…

▼…he dipped his spoon in for a taste.

Though he’d now finished his chicken, so was unable to try it with the honey maple syrup-enhanced ice cream, the drizzle of sweet sauce elevated everything into pure dessert territory. The slightly sweet biscuit, sweet soft-serve and added sweetness from the honey maple syrup created the ultimate triple-sweet treat.

Mr Sato dialled up the bliss levels by enjoying it all with a hot coffee on the side, which helped to create the ultimate dessert experience. Trying the soft serve multiple ways is the key to ultimate enjoyment, and Mr Sato highly recommends trying it if you can.

As of now, Mr Sato was able to confirm that the soft-serve is currently available at the Akihabara and Asakusa branches in Tokyo, as well as the Minami-machida Grandberry Park branch. There doesn’t appear to be any official information about the rollout, so he recommends checking social media and confirming availability with each branch before visiting.

title: Is hamburger patty ramen a case of too many good things in one bowl? Let’s find out! [Taste test]
description: Far away from Japan’s most touristy neighborhoods is a daring fusion dish from a very old-school restaurant. Generally speaking, ramen and hamburger patties are pretty far apart from each other on the eastern-or-western culinary spectrum. Personally, we’re big fans of both here at SoraNews24, but it’s generally sort of an either/or question as to which […]
content:
Far away from Japan’s most touristy neighborhoods is a daring fusion dish from a very old-school restaurant.

Generally speaking, ramen and hamburger patties are pretty far apart from each other on the eastern-or-western culinary spectrum. Personally, we’re big fans of both here at SoraNews24, but it’s generally sort of an either/or question as to which one of those cravings we’re going to satisfy in single meal.

So imagine the surprise of our Japanese-language reporter Takuya Inaba when he recently discovered the existence of hamburger steak ramen.

That might sound like the sort of thing you’d encounter at a tourist-trap eatery near downtown Tokyo’s Shibuya crossing, but instead we came across this innovative dish at Koryu, a decidedly old-school ramen restaurant not far from the shore of Lake Sagami in the town of Sagamihara in Kanagawa, the prefecture that borders Tokyo on the capital’s southern side.

From its exterior, Koryu (whose name translates as “Lake Dragon”), does not look like a place that chases after gimmicky food trends, and that vibe continues once you step inside. This restaurant has been serving up ramen in this location for roughly 40 years, and it has the sort of rustically inviting, at-home atmosphere that makes you understandingly nod your head at how long it’s been in business.

Flipping through the menu, we first saw a page with old standards like shoyu (soy sauce broth) and miso ramen, with prices starting at just 680 yen (US$4.30).

But then we got to the section where the more deluxe options are listed, and there it was.

▼ Hamburger steak ramen

Fusion recipes like this are always a bit of a gamble, but at a still-reasonable price of 1,080 yen, we decided to roll the dice and order it. As Ryuko’s owner, who operates the restaurant by himself most days, began preparing our hamburger steak ramen, we braced ourselves for an utterly bizarre-looking bowl of noodles to be placed before us…

…but it turned out to be shockingly normal looking. Not plain or unappealing, mind you, but largely in keeping with what you’d expect to see in a bowl of ramen, with negi (green onions), menma (fermented bamboo shoots), seaweed, kinshi tamago (thin strands of egg), and a swirly naruto fish cake.

Following standard ramen-tasting protocol, Takuya started with a sip of the broth. It was flavorful, with what he describes as strong umami sensations and a mild saltiness which still came to an incredibly clean finish in its flavor profile, leading him to think the pork stock must be made by cooking on low heat for a very long time.

OK, now it was time to take a clearer look at the hamburger steak, which Takuya could perceive subtly floating underneath the egg. Using his spoon, he brushed the strands aside.

Ah, there you are! Obviously, the hamburger steak didn’t say hi or otherwise audibly announce its presence, but it immediately demanded attention by nature of being something you just don’t see in this environment, like if there had been a polar bear soaking in the broth.

However, after the broth the next thing ramen fans say you’re supposed to taste is the noodles, so Takuya did what he could to put the hamburger steak out of his mind for the moment.

The noodles, which the owner makes himself in-house, had a nice, springy texture to them, and Takuya was blown away by how good the menma, which the owner also personally prepares, tasted.

But at this point, Takuya couldn’t contain his curiosity any longer, so it was time to try the hamburger steak.

Balanced on his spoon, he was happily surprised at just how big it was. Now thoroughly soaked with broth, he wondered if this mix of eastern and western elements really could work together, so he took a bite…

…and discovered that, yeah, this is honestly good stuff!

Unlike with a hamburger or a standard hamburger steak set meal, the patty here isn’t slathered with ketchup, barbecue sauce, or any other condiments. Instead, the delicious flavor of the meat itself is what gets full play on your taste buds, and by nature of being less fatty and oily than many of the chashu pork strips that are the most common meaty topping for ramen, the broth’s inherently appealing flavors aren’t muddled in any way either.

So it turns out that just like hamburger patties can work as a sushi topping, they can work as a ramen topping too. Again, since Ryuko is a one-man-run restaurant, waits can get long around peak lunch and dinner hours, so we’d recommend avoiding those times, and the location does mean that experiencing this unique dish for yourself will take a bit of planning, but with the nearby Lake Sagami Illumination Christmas light display making its return later this month, there are two reasons to make the day trip from Tokyo out to this part of Japan.

title: Historical-themed illumination display returns to Osaka Castle this winter
description: The greatest lights in history and the greatest history in lights. I’ve never been too good at history, mainly because I’m terrible at remembering names and dates. But I find when it’s presented in ways other than fact sheets, I can remember what happened a lot more clearly. If you’re like me, then an upcoming […]
content:
The greatest lights in history and the greatest history in lights.

I’ve never been too good at history, mainly because I’m terrible at remembering names and dates. But I find when it’s presented in ways other than fact sheets, I can remember what happened a lot more clearly. If you’re like me, then an upcoming event in Osaka might be just what you need to handle the long and complex history of Japan.

From 20 November to 14 February, the Nishinomaru Garden of Osaka Castle will be brilliantly lit up. Although an illumination display might just sound like a bunch of lights, they tend to go really all out with them in Japan, and the Osaka Castle Illuminage is no exception.

This year’s theme is “Unification of the Realm, Shogun – A Story in Light,” and boasts almost as many lights as it has subtitles, fittingly using the castle that noted warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi once resided in as a backdrop. In a nutshell, Toyotomi was one of The Three Unifiers of Japan, having worked his way up from the peasant class to grasp control of the entire country. He ordered the construction of Osaka Castle as a base of operations for about a decade before his death in 1598.

This illumination event goes far beyond that, however, with an array of dazzling displays both educational and fantastical. Upon entering the garden, guests will follow a corridor of 66 lanterns to help you feel like you’re right in the light show, rather than looking at it from afar.

Then, there’s an array of taiko drums, bearing the paulownia crest of the Toyotomi clan, which is still used by the Japanese government today. The drums are meant to be a symbol of the strength the entire country has when working together as one, while also providing the atmosphere of a traditional festival, where these types of drums are often employed.

Deeper inside is a light display in the shape of a large nanban trading ship. It is often pointed out that “nanban” literally means “Southern barbarian” and was used for Portuguese traders who successfully reached Japan. However, it was more of a generalized term inherited from Chinese, and many of the goods, arts, and technology brought in by these traders were highly regarded. That’s not to say the “barbarian” label wasn’t used pejoratively as well. There was plenty of discrimination to go around back then too.

Speaking of which, the fashions brought in from foreign traders were often well received and had a gradual influence on Japanese culture. It’s something that can be seen in a line of light-based illustrations showcasing how people dressed from 1615 through the large-scale Westernization of Japan in the early 20th century and to the present day. 

The journey ends at a plaza-like area with neon light displays featuring an assortment of images from Japanese culture, past and present. It’s the perfect place to take a commemorative photo of your visit.

This year will also see two new additions to Osaka Castle Illuminage. First, there’s a butterfly swing that is likely to see a lot of action. When rocking back and forth on this four-meter-tall swing set, the wings of the giant butterfly on top move.

There’s also a small enclosure that you can enter. Its walls are made of dozens of pinwheels, so when a breeze comes by, they’ll spin and scatter the lights in unexpected patterns.

The Osaka Castle Illuminage will be open every day during the period from 5 p.m. to 10 p.m. rain or shine. Just remember that although much of Osaka Castle is free to walk around, the Nishinomaru Garden section charges an admission of 2,000 yen (US$13) for adults and 1,000 yen for kids, but babies get in for free. There’s also a really good cake shop nearby if you need to kill some time before it gets dark.

Check it out if you can and learn some history or be doomed to repeat it. Just like that guy, whatsisface from the 17th or 18th century.

title: Starbucks Japan reveals new Joyful Capsule gacha toy release date

content:
The wait for these Japan-exclusive collectibles is almost over.

Back in July, Starbucks surprised customers in Japan with the news that it would be releasing a never-before-seen “Joyful Capsule” collection. Consisting of nine miniature plush charms across two collections, the range is Starbucks’ first-ever gacha capsule toy collection, and though it was first slated to be released in August, the launch was postponed out of consideration for victims of the 28 July earthquake in Kumamoto Prefecture.

Now, Starbucks has announced that the new release date has been set for 18 November, and unlike the previous plan, which limited sales to only 19 Starbucks stores in Tokyo, the standard collection will now be available at stores right around the country.

This is great news for Starbucks fans, who have been patiently waiting to get their hands on the collection. Each gacha capsule contains a palm-sized plush charm measuring approximately 5-8 centimetres (2-3 inches), with a handy hook attachment that allows you to easily pop it onto a bag or pouch, or even connect it to other charms in the series.

The contents of each capsule are random, so you won’t know which design you’ve got until you open it, and there are five designs in the standard collection, inspired by some of Starbucks’ most recognisable menu items.

▼ Double Tall Latte (To Go)

▼ Caramel Macchiato (For Here)

▼ Tokyo Roast

▼ Matcha Cream Frappuccino

▼ Sugar Doughnut

In addition to the standard collection, there will be a special Starbucks Reserve Joyful Capsule range released on the same day at the Starbucks Reserve Roastery Tokyo. This exclusive range features four plush charms inspired by drinks and food items associated with the Roastery, giving fans the chance to take home a little memento of the special store.

▼ Caffe Americano (To Go)

▼ Caffe Latte (For Here)

▼ Tokyo Roastery Microblend

▼ Cornetti Crema

While each capsule in the standard range costs 880 yen (US$5.70), the Reserve collection is priced slightly higher, at 1,100 yen each. Whichever collection you choose, though, purchases are limited to two capsules per transaction for each collection, to allow as many customers as possible to own a piece of the collection.

The method of sale may also vary between stores, with some using traditional capsule toy machines and others selling the capsules over the counter. The charms are intended for ages 15 and up, and will only be available while stocks last.

title: Japanese drivers reminded to look out for drunk people passed out on the road this holiday season
description: As if driving in Japan isn’t hard enough. As the year gradually draws to a close, it’s the time for many organizations to hold their year-end parties. Although many younger people have been increasingly distancing themselves from overindulging in alcohol, drinking is still a major part of these year-end festivities. As a result, this is […]
content:
As if driving in Japan isn’t hard enough.

As the year gradually draws to a close, it’s the time for many organizations to hold their year-end parties. Although many younger people have been increasingly distancing themselves from overindulging in alcohol, drinking is still a major part of these year-end festivities.

As a result, this is also the prime time of year to find business people passed out on benches, the side of the road, or, more problematically, right in the middle of roads. People passing out on roads, or “rojo nekomi” as it’s known in Japan, is not new but a lot of attention has been given to it in recent years after people started heading back to the bars in a post-COVID world.

In 2023, about 32 percent of nighttime traffic fatalities involving pedestrians in Tokyo were people who fell asleep on the street. However, alcohol shouldn’t take all the blame for this either. According to the National Police Agency, only 70 percent of rojo nekomi incidents were connected to alcohol, with rising temperatures and an aging population leading to other health issues like heatstroke causing people to faint on the road.

▼ The Japan Auto Federation released a video examining how easy it is for drivers to spot and respond to a person sleeping on the road at night. It’s in Japanese but fairly easy to get the gist of, regardless of the language.

In response, various taxi companies have begun working hand-in-hand with the police forces of 32 prefectures to keep an eye out for unconscious people on the streets. The programs seem to be effective as well, because on 9 November, a pair of Tokyo cab drivers were officially commended for assisting street sleepers in two separate incidents.

Seijo Police Station invited 70-year-old Yoshitatsu Miura and 28-year-old Kazuki Yamamoto to honor their efforts in rescuing two people from potential death. During the ceremony, Miura explained that he encountered the body at about 2 a.m. and shone his headlights on the person to make them highly visible to other motorists while he called the emergency number for help.

In Yamamoto’s case, he felt disappointed that while he was helping the unconscious person, there were other people walking along the street at the time. Some just chose to look the other way. 

Online comments were happy everything turned out fine in these instances, while some admitted they might not have the courage to get involved like these drivers had.

“Everyone was lucky this had a happy ending. If the drivers had hit those people, their lives would have been ruined too.”
“Papers are nice and all, but give them some money for that!”
“I saw an elderly man sleeping on the road while drunk. I asked if he was OK, but he just yelled at me, so I just moved him out of the way and left. From now on, I’m going to ignore anyone I see like that.”
“I wonder what the cutoff is for getting commendations? Tons of people report stuff to the police, after all.”
“It’s a common thing in Tokyo near the end of the year.”
“If you get so drunk that you sleep on the road, then alcohol isn’t for you.”
“I don’t want to get involved, so I probably wouldn’t touch them, but I think I could call someone…”
“People who get drunk and fall asleep on the street should be penalized too.”

Punishing those who fall asleep on the streets due to drunkenness is a tricky issue. Unlike in Western countries, being even extremely drunk in public is not illegal as long as the intoxicated person is not harassing, assaulting, or damaging anyone or anything. If someone is passed out due to alcohol, the police will detain them for their own protection rather than to arrest them for a crime.

That being said, obstructing traffic by lying down or sitting on the road is a crime, punishable by a maximum fine of 50,000 yen (US$317). The problem here is that it’s pretty hard to prove intent on the part of the sleeping person if they’re unconscious at the time of the offense.

In Okinawa, where the warm climate has helped to make rojo nekomi a more pervasive problem, the police have been more aggressive and have begun charging repeat offenders with traffic obstruction charges.

▼ This news report features harrowing dashcam footage of a driver stopping right in front of a person sleeping on the road in Itoman, Okinawa.

As far as civil litigation goes, the liability for damages or injuries that occurred is considered 30 percent the sleeper’s if during the day and 50 percent if at night. But regardless of how these incidents play out, no good comes of it for anyone involved, so stay safe either by drinking in moderation and getting a safe ride home or by driving at a reasonable speed at night with the appropriate lights in use.

title: 41.5 percent of surveyed Japanese middle schoolers don’t think more immigration benefits society
description: This isn’t a cut-and-dry case of Japanese kids simply becoming more socially conservative, though. Internationalism is becoming an increasingly discussed topic in Japan, as the country’s indigenous population contracts and its number of foreign-national residents increases. This shift is happening quickly enough to be noticed not only by adults comparing the current demographics to how […]
content:
This isn’t a cut-and-dry case of Japanese kids simply becoming more socially conservative, though.

Internationalism is becoming an increasingly discussed topic in Japan, as the country’s indigenous population contracts and its number of foreign-national residents increases. This shift is happening quickly enough to be noticed not only by adults comparing the current demographics to how they were decades ago, but by adolescents too, and a recent study shows that many of them don’t necessarily see Japan’s growing foreign population as a good thing.

University of Tokyo sociology professor Norihiro Nihei conducts a periodic survey of all students at 10 middle schools in Tokyo and the surrounding area in order to track changes in their attitudes regarding social issues. The students are presented with a series of statements, then asked whether they agree or disagree with them. One of those statements is “An increase in the number of foreigners living in Japan will bring many benefits to society,” and in the most recent survey, more than 40 percent said they do not agree.

An increase in the number of foreigners living in Japan will bring many benefits to society
● Do not agree at all: 9.6 percent of respondents
● Somewhat disagree: 31.9 percent
● Somewhat agree: 39.8 percent
● Strongly agree: 18.6 percent

The percentage of students disagreeing with the notion that immigration would be beneficial to Japanese society nearly doubled between the most recent survey, the data for which was collected in 2025, and the previous iteration of the survey, which was carried out in 2023.

An increase in the number of foreigners living in Japan will bring many benefits to society (2023 results)
● Do not agree at all: 3.96 percent of respondents
● Somewhat disagree: 18.3 percent
● Somewhat agree: 50.4 percent
● Strongly agree: 27.4 percent

That jump from 22.26 percent who didn’t see increasing immigration as a major positive for society in 2023 to 41.5 percent in 2025 is significant. Nihei is quick to say, though, that this doesn’t signal an across-the-board shift towards right-wing attitudes for young people in Japan. As a matter of fact, he asserts that the way the labels “liberal” and “conservative” are used in Japan and the English-speaking world don’t always perfectly align, and so he wants to put a finer point on how the survey is applying the terms.

For the purposes of the survey, Nihei examines what he describes as three indicators of liberal orientation: democratic orientation, tolerance, and autonomous orientation, which the study checks for by presenting a statement representing each. Among them, there were no dramatic drops since the previous survey.

Total percentage of agree/strongly agree responses for:
● Rules should be decided through everyone’s discussion. (democratic orientation)
2025: 96 percent
2023: 95.1 percent
● I can accept people with different ways of thinking. (tolerance)
2025: 91.6 percent
2023: 92.1 percent
● It is important to stay true to oneself in any situation. (autonomous orientation)
2025: 83 percent
2023: 87.1 percent

There were, however, some large increases in agreement to statements that, within the scope of the study, Nihei cites as indicators of conservative or right-wing orientations of authoritarianism, patriotism, and xenophobia.

Total percentage of agree/strongly agree responses for:
● I should follow the instructions of teachers and seniors rather than my own thoughts. (authoritarianism)
2025: 61.3 percent
2023: 57.4 percent
● It is important to love one’s country. (patriotism)
2025: 86.8 percent
2023: 76.9 percent

Total percentage of disagree/strongly disagree responses for:
● An increase in the number of foreigners living in Japan will bring many benefits to society. (xenophobia-related attitudes)
2025: 41.5 percent
2023: 23.1 percent

It might seem like an odd combination to have continuing extremely high-expressed support for accepting other people’s way of thinking and collectively deciding on the rules while at the same time having a jump in uncertainty as to whether or not more foreigners living in Japan is a good thing for society, but there’s one other factor the survey examines, which Nihei calls “rule strictness,” measured by the participant’s reactions to the statement “People who do not follow rules should be severely punished,” which 70.8 percent of respondents agreed with in 2022. In 2025, the percentage rose to 79.3 percent.

The idea of strict enforcement of regulations might seem like something from the conservative school of thought, and Nihei does recognize that such strictness could be seen as the opposite of tolerance, which he treats as a liberal value. However, in an example of one of the many ways conservative and social values may not consist of the same baskets of attitudes in one society as they do in another, Nihei says:

“This concept sits on a different axis from the liberal/conservative spectrum. Literally standing at the opposite pole of tolerance, it appears non-liberal on the surface. On the other hand, rule compliance has historically served as a prerequisite for managing a fair society by restraining arbitrary uses of power, thus forming an essential element of liberalism. This is also linked to constitutionalism, having played a key role for the left as well in various forms, such as refusing to tolerate ‘slush-fund lawmakers.’”

Taken together, the combination of, to borrow the survey’s terminology, continuing high tolerance at the same time that both xenophobia and rule strictness are increasing could be construed as reflecting a change in Japanese young people’s perception as to how willing foreigners are to follow Japan’s laws and social customs. Though Nihei’s report on the most recent survey’s results don’t delve into this issue, high-profile crimes such as theft and assault involving foreign perpetrators used to be few and far between, but have become not-uncommon occurrences in recent years, and could be contributing to a diminished image of foreign residents’ likelihood of integrating into the peaceful, orderly norms that have long been the default for most Japanese communities. That sort of stigma could be especially influential on Japanese children, who might not have any foreigners among their peers, as Japan’s foreign population has far more adults than minors, and so might not have any personal acquaintances to counteract the bad examples that become major news stories.

The survey being conducted in the Tokyo area could also be affecting the results, as one of the most commonly pointed-to concrete ways in which Japan could benefit from increased immigration is help in filling labor shortages and preventing population vacuums in smaller communities whose Japanese residents are moving to the big cities, but those aren’t problems that Tokyo and its immediate neighbors are really struggling with. The current state of the economy is also a likely factor in the growing skepticism about immigration among the surveyed middle schoolers. Proponents of increased immigration within the Japanese government have been advocating for expanded support for foreign residents to promote smoother integration into Japanese society. Unfortunately, this is occurring at the same time that rapidly rising costs of living and stagnant wages are putting the pinch on Japan’s middle and lower classes. Middle schoolers probably aren’t tracking consumer price indexes and sifting through government budget proposals, but many probably do have a sense that money is getting tighter for their or their classmates’ families, and so the idea of an increased focus on helping foreign residents coinciding with a decrease in their perceived willingness to follow the rules might not sit well with many of the survey participants.

It’s very important, though, to keep in mind that 41.5 percent of the surveyed middle schoolers saying they don’t think an increase in foreign residents will be beneficial to society also means that 58.5 percent of them, the majority, do think that increased immigration would be a good thing. In other words, xenophobia isn’t the default attitude among Japanese kids, and hopefully whatever factors are contributing to the bump of the needle in that direction can be resolved while that’s still the case.

title: Tokyo neighborhood adds new “smart trash cans” to deal with increasing amounts of tourist litter
description: A high-tech part of Tokyo gets some high-tech help in addressing an overtourism problem and responding to a common traveler complaint. Downtown Tokyo’s Akihabara neighborhood is already one of the most popular tourism destinations for travelers in Japan, by nature of being the country’s center of anime and video game fan culture, and a couple […]
content:
A high-tech part of Tokyo gets some high-tech help in addressing an overtourism problem and responding to a common traveler complaint.

Downtown Tokyo’s Akihabara neighborhood is already one of the most popular tourism destinations for travelers in Japan, by nature of being the country’s center of anime and video game fan culture, and a couple of new additions to the district are sure to be instant crowd pleasers too. We’re not talking about a new multi-level arcade or manga merch specialty store, though, but a bunch of new public trash cans.

Japan’s relative lack of trash receptacles in public spaces has long been among the top complaint from foreign visitors to the country, and it’s an issue that exists even in the most densely developed parts of Tokyo. In recent years, there’s been a noticeable increase in the amount of litter to be seen in the city’s most heavily touristed areas, including Akihabara.

▼ A pile of trash on the sidewalk in Akihabara in January of this year

Using funds from the municipal government’s Tokyo Green Up Action subsidy program, Chiyoda Ward, which Akihabara is part of, has acquired 22 SmaGO “smart trash cans” from Tokyo-based tech company Forcetec. Fittingly for Akihabara’s image as a high-tech part of town, these receptacles are actually public trash compactors, using solar power to condense their contents down to one-fifth of their original size. They can also utilize a cloud network to inform maintenance workers of how full the bins currently are, allowing for more efficient coordination of trash pickups.

▼ As is usually the case in Japan, different types of trash go in different containers, so make sure to sort your stuff before you toss it in.

The SmaGO trash cans went into service at 10 locations in Akihabara, clustered around Akihabara Station (秋葉原駅 in the map below) and along Chuo-dori (中央通り), the major shopping street in the neighborhood.

The move follows new ordinances requiring more publicly accessible trash cans, and stricter penalties for not using them, which recently went into effect across town in the Shibuya neighborhood. Both districts’ responses to increasing amounts of litter do make one feel a little sad that the current crop of visitors evidently isn’t as concerned with Japan’s customary etiquette norm of carrying your trash home with you if there’s no public place to dispose of it, but hopefully the new initiatives will result in a return to cleaner streets.

title: Why people in Japan hardly ever say “sayonara,” and what they say instead
description: Everyone knows that sayonara means goodbye in Japanese, but goodbye in Japan doesn’t always mean you need to say it. You don’t have to be an anime otaku, foodie with a penchant for matcha and wagyu, or obsessive linguistics enthusiast that know that sayonara means “goodbye” in Japanese. Like loco in Spanish and merci in French, […]
content:
Everyone knows that sayonara means goodbye in Japanese, but goodbye in Japan doesn’t always mean you need to say it.

You don’t have to be an anime otaku, foodie with a penchant for matcha and wagyu, or obsessive linguistics enthusiast that know that sayonara means “goodbye” in Japanese. Like loco in Spanish and merci in French, sayonara is one of those words that’s so well known internationally that it’s widely understood even by people without any personal connection to its home-country culture.

And yet, living in Japan, you’ll very rarely hear anyone actually say sayonara (unless you happen to be in a pre-college school, where students of such ages say it to their teachers at the end of the school day). As a matter of fact, when someone did say it to us the other day, it was startling, even if it was also very appropriate to the specific circumstances that was taking place.

But wait, if sayonara isn’t a commonly used phrase, how do people in Japan end conversations? Does one person just wander off once they think the topic has run its course, and the value that Japanese culture places on tacit understanding means that you’re just supposed to infer that the other person said goodbye to you inside their heart?

▼ Wait, Linguistics Samurai! I still had something I needed to tell you!

Nope. Japanese actually has several other phrases that take sayonara’s place in the vast majority of daily situations. Let’s take a look at a few, and then circle back to why sayonara usually isn’t used.

One of the most common ways to say goodbye when speaking to friends or peers in social situations is ja, which means “if” or “then.” That might seem like a pretty random choice of vocabulary, but there is a logical reason for it, which is that it’s a shortened version of sore ja, meaning “if it’s like that,” or, rendered more naturally in English “in that case” or “well then.”

In this situation, sore ja is itself a pared-down version of phrases such as sore ja, kore de kaerimasu (“well then, I’m heading home”), sore ja, ikanakya” (“well then, I’ve got to get going”), and the like. But if you don’t want to get into the nitty-gritty of why you’re saying goodbye, Japanese social norms allow you to opt out of the explanation and just say “ja.” Used completely by itself, though, ja can sound a little curt, so to make it a little cordial the all-purpose emphasizer ne, or na among male speakers, is often tacked onto the end.

Speaking of adding things after ja, another option for that is mata, the Japanese word for “again.” In this case, it’s included as an abbreviation of things such as mata aimashou (“let’s get together again [sometime]”) or mata ashita (“[see you] again tomorrow”). And to multiply our options even further, if you want to sound a little more polished and polite, you can replace ja with dewa, a more formal word with the same meaning.

Mixing and matching these elements will give you all sorts of common ways of saying “goodbye” in Japanese that you’ll hear much, much more frequently than sayonara, such as:
● ja / ja ne / ja na
● dewa
● sore ja / sore dewa
● mata / mata ne / mata na
● sore ja, mata / sore ja, mata ne / sore ja, mata na
● dewa, mata ne / dewa, mata na

There are two other Japanese phrases which also don’t translate literally as “goodbye” but regularly get used where we’d say that in English. One of them is otsukarasama desu, which, as we’ve discussed before, more or less means “you must be tired,” but which is commonly said between coworkers when going home at the end of the day, since you’ve both put in a full day of work. Similarly, if you’re going home while someone else is still working, the custom is to tell them osaki ni shitsurei shimasu, meaning “excuse me for going home before you,” which can be shortened down to just osaki ni if you’re on friendly terms with one another.

But even knowing all that, sayonara does still mean “goodbye,” so why isn’t it said very often? Because sayonara has a very weighty nuance to it, so much so that it’s mainly used for situations where it’s not just goodbye, but possibly goodbye forever, or at the very least where there’s a very real possibility that you’ll never meet again.

▼ Hearing “sayonara” at the end of a first date is a strong sign that there’s not going to be a second.

Because of that, sayonara isn’t something classmates say to each other after grabbing ramen together. It’s what they might say to each other at graduation if they’re all going off to different colleges and there’s no real guarantee they’re going to meet up again. You wouldn’t say sayonara to your coworker Tanaka-san when you clock out on a Friday evening, but you might say it to him at his going away party before his permanent transfer to an overseas office.

▼ If your coworker walks out of the office while waving and saying “Sayonara!”, there’s a good chance she just quit.

In other words, when someone does tell you sayonara, it tends to stick with you, because it’s a sign of parting that might be permanent. When someone said it to us the other day, it was a bittersweet moment, so who did we hear it from?

The workers at Cold Stone in the city of Kamakura, the very last branch of the chain in all of east Japan, which we visited for one last ice cream treat shortly before it closed on October 31.

While he was waiting for his order, our reporter Mr. Sato briefly chatted with the staff about the shop shutting down, and when they handed him his ice cream, they told him thank you, and also “sayonara.” This is Cold Stone’s second time to leave east Japan, and it wouldn’t be a shock if the company decides not to ever take a third shot at it, and that situation was reflected in the employees’ choice of words.

Now, none of this means that there’s a taboo against saying sayonara, or that it’s an old-fashioned phrase that feels out of place in the modern world. Sayonara does, though, carry a lot of emotional significance, so it’s a special phrase for special circumstances.

content:
With tourists’ and residents’ feelings about minpaku racing in opposite directions, wards add new local ordinances onto national laws.

“Short-term private vacation lodging” is a bit of a mouthful, and while “Airbnb-style rentals” is more concise, it singles out just one company in what’s become a rapidly expanding sector of traveler accommodations. So today, let’s just call them “minpaku,” the term used in Japanese to describe rentals for travelers that weren’t originally zoned or constructed as hotels.

Minpaku have been rapidly rising in popularity over the past few years. While the idea of staying in a converted home while on vacation has limited appeal to most Japanese travelers, foreign tourists have shown plenty of enthusiasm for minpaku, especially when coming to Japan in a group of friends or family members who want more communal space for their party than conventional hotels offer. That growing popularity with foreign tourists has simultaneously made minpaku’s presence increasingly unwelcome among local Japanese residents, however, and new ordinances mean that all 23 central wards of Tokyo have now introduced additional rules restricting or limiting their operation, including new bans on accepting guests on weekdays.

Houses and apartments are built very close to one another in Japan’s residential neighborhoods. and that creates a sort of etiquette-deterrence situation between long-term residents. The close proximity means that any excess noise or trash generated by one neighbor is likely to affect everyone around them, and vice versa, so residents generally try to stay quiet and clean as a show of mutual consideration, with the baseline tacit agreement of “I won’t cause problems for you, and you won’t cause problems for me.” The importance of maintaining polite long-term relationships within the community doesn’t apply to short-term renters, though, who’ll probably be gone in a few days’ time, and far too often ill-mannered minpaku guests party noisily late into the night, litter in the common-use areas of the buildings they stay in and on the surrounding streets, and otherwise.

Minpaku lodgings in Japan started off as a bit of a cottage industry, and the sector managed to build up significant momentum before widespread regulatory measures were put in place. Under the Private Lodging Business Law, minpaku are not allowed to accept guests for more than 180 nights in a calendar year, but many local municipalities have placed additional regulations on top of that. Most recently, Tokyo’s Kita Ward became the city’s 23rd ward to pass its own. As of January 7, Kita Ward will ban the opening of new minpaku in residential areas in which the homeowner is not present when guests are staying in the unit. Requiring the homeowner to be present should, theoretically, increase the minpaku operator’s connection, and personal responsibility, to the surrounding community, creating an accessible contact point for complaints from neighbors or regulatory enforcement by the ward, while discouraging management by remote companies whose facelessness makes it easier for them to ignore grievances.

▼ It’s harder for management to brush off complaints when they have to deal with them in-person.

Tokyo’s Taito Ward is also tightening restrictions on minpaku. As of October 1, no new minpaku within the ward will be allowed to accept guests on weekdays, and no new minpaku of any kind will be allowed to open in parts of the ward which are zoned for residential-use only. Taito is also taking action against four minpaku owners who collectively operate eight units within the ward. By law, minpaku operators are required to submit reports on a minpaku’s number of guests and nights in operation every two months, but the owners filed no reports at all for the eight properties for the period between December of 2025 and May of 2026. Taito is now giving the owners approximately three weeks to submit the required documents, and says that failure to do so will result in the owners’ names being publicly announced, followed by forced closures of the minpaku if the non-compliance continues.

Other parts of Tokyo are going even farther in their attempts to address residents’ growing irritation at minpaku. Shinjuku Ward, for example, is looking to add legislation that would not only designate areas within it as off-limits for new minpaku, but which would also force currently existing minpaku within them to shut down.

In total, Tokyo’s 23 central wards account for roughly 40 percent of all the minpaku in Japan, so it’s likely that other cities will be watching the effectiveness of these countermeasures very closely, and possibly basing their future policies on them in an effort to stave off resident complaints before any such friction with minpaku operators/guests occurs.

Source: Taito Ward (1, 2), Kita Ward, Asahi Shimbun, Tokyo MX, Mainichi Shimbun
